summary: Describes common practices for gateways that interwork between the telephone network (PSTN) and SIP networks. It sorts the uses of such gateways, gives use cases, and identifies mechanisms needed, including encapsulating PSTN signaling inside SIP and translating it into SIP. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Old phone lines and internet calls speak different languages. This document describes how translating gateways between them should work so calls behave the same way everywhere.

questions: how do pstn to sip gateways work
what is isup encapsulation in sip
what is the difference between encapsulation and translation in sip-t
subtitle: How phone-network gateways and SIP networks can interwork without losing telephony features or routability.

tldr.problem: A SIP telephony network must interwork with the PSTN, but SIP alone cannot carry all the SS7 ISUP information that telephone features need, and SIP proxies cannot read ISUP in order to route calls.
tldr.mechanism: SIP-T encapsulates the ISUP message in a multipart MIME body and also translates key ISUP parameters, such as the called number, into SIP headers. It uses the INFO method for mid-call signaling.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a framework and best current practice that sets out gateway roles and points to the documents that supply the actual mechanisms. It is not a new protocol.

today: RFC 3372 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 63) and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It describes context and architectures and refers to other documents for the detailed mechanisms.

sections.title: The PSTN-SIP Interworking Problem
sections.content:
SIP is an application-layer control protocol that establishes, modifies and terminates multimedia sessions or calls, and it is one of the key protocols for Voice over IP. A SIP telephony network cannot exist in isolation, so it has to interwork with the PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network). The popularity of PSTN-SIP gateways motivated this set of common practices, so that behavior is consistent across implementations.

Two properties matter. Feature transparency means services such as call waiting or freephone numbers, carried in Signaling System No. 7 (SS7), should work over SIP without a debilitating difference in user experience, and SS7 information should reach trusted parties in the SIP network without loss. Routability means a SIP request for a call must carry enough in its headers, such as the dialed number, for proxy servers to route it.

The RFC's Table 1 pairs each requirement with a SIP-T function: encapsulation of ISUP in the SIP body, translation of ISUP information into SIP headers, and the INFO method for mid-call ISUP messages. It focuses on SS7 ISUP only, and it is a framework that points to the documents providing the mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone call that starts on an old phone line and ends on an internet phone needs a translator in the middle. The translator must pass along everything important and still tell the call where to go.

sections.title: Agents and Call Flows
sections.content:
SIP-T is not a new protocol. It is a set of mechanisms for interfacing traditional telephone signaling with SIP, used wherever a SIP network meets the PSTN. The agents are the PSTN, IP endpoints (gateways, SIP phones and interface points where policy is enforced) and proxy servers. A gateway converts between signaling protocols and between circuit-switched and packet-switched audio. Large gateway clusters are called Media Gateway Controllers (MGCs).

That gives three working call flows, plus a fourth that does not need SIP-T:

  • PSTN to PSTN (SIP bridging): the originating gateway preserves ISUP in the SIP request, and the terminating gateway reuses it when signaling to the PSTN.
  • PSTN to IP: the SIP phone has no use for the encapsulated ISUP and ignores it.
  • IP to PSTN: there is no encapsulated ISUP, so the terminating gateway only translates SIP headers into ISUP parameters.
  • IP to IP: pure SIP, with no PSTN interworking.

The originator does not choose among these flows. Each call is routed by the SIP network independently and may end up in any of them.
sections.plainLanguage: A call can go phone line to phone line through the internet, phone line to internet phone, or internet phone to phone line. The network works out which one as it goes.

sections.title: Originator, Terminator and Intermediary Roles
sections.content:
The originator generates the SIP INVITE. When a call starts in the PSTN, the gateway is the originator and must encapsulate the ISUP, identify its variant (ETSI, ANSI and so on), usually by adding a multipart MIME body, and fill the INVITE headers from ISUP parameters. For example, the To header can reflect the Called Party Number of the ISUP IAM. If the originator is a gateway that received ISUP, it must always do both encapsulation and translation. Ordinary SIP phones are not expected to generate ISUP.

The terminator is a standard SIP user agent, either a gateway or a SIP phone. A gateway extracts the encapsulated ISUP and uses it as a template, overwrites values it can translate from SIP headers, and applies local policy. With no encapsulated ISUP, it uses a canonical pre-populated template for that message type. A SIP phone typically ignores the ISUP but must handle multipart MIME and unknown MIME types gracefully.

Intermediaries, mainly proxy servers, route on routable elements such as the Request-URI and Route headers. The ISUP variant itself could become one. If the two PSTN sides use incompatible variants, a proxy can have the call converted between variants, which costs call-setup time, or hand the call to a gateway that ignores the encapsulated ISUP and uses only the SIP headers, which gives up ISUP transparency.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender packs the call details in a box and also writes the address on the outside. The receiver may open the box or just read the address. The post office only reads the address.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Translation and Mid-Call Signaling
sections.content:
SIP-T uses core SIP as defined in RFC 3261. Its extra pieces are:

  • Encapsulation: multipart MIME bodies let one SIP message hold several payloads, such as SDP and ISUP. The ISUP MIME type lets a recipient see the ISUP variant quickly. One scheme is in RFC 3204.
  • Translation: this has two parts. Message mapping decides which ISUP message goes with which SIP message (an IAM must be sent on receipt of an INVITE, a REL for BYE). Parameter mapping carries information such as the Called Party Number into the SIP To header field and Request-URI.
  • Mid-call signaling: pure SIP cannot carry mid-call control information, so the INFO method (RFC 2976) should be used. INFO is not suitable for overlap dialing, and the RFC does not recommend it for mid-call DTMF signals, pointing to RFC 2833 instead.

Translation is tricky because intermediaries can change SIP headers. The headers and the encapsulated ISUP can then disagree, and part of the encapsulated ISUP may become irrelevant and obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: Translation is like writing the important bits on the envelope, and encapsulation is like tucking the whole original letter inside. INFO is a way to pass notes while the call is already going.

sections.title: Content Negotiation for ISUP Bodies
sections.content:
A SIP-T request can carry both SDP and ISUP in one multipart message. Traditionally, a terminating device that does not support multipart/mixed or the ISUP MIME type rejects the request with 415 Unsupported Media Type, and the originator has to resend without the ISUP. The RFC calls this cumbersome and wants a way for the originator to mark which bodies are required and which are optional, using multipart/mixed and the Content-Disposition header to express criticality.

It shows three examples:

  • ISUP marked handling=optional: the receiver accepts the INVITE whether or not it can process the ISUP.
  • ISUP marked handling=required but only preferred: the receiver replies 415, and the originator resends with SDP only.
  • ISUP mandatory for call setup: after the 415, the originator sends the request to a different user agent instead.
sections.plainLanguage: If you mail a package with a part the receiver cannot use, the receiver can ignore it if you said it was optional. If it was essential, you try a different receiver.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SIP-T can serve as an interdomain signaling mechanism subject to trust relationships between administrative domains. In many legal environments the distribution of ISUP is restricted to licensed carriers, and SIP-T bridges carrier signaling with end-user signaling. Any domain running SIP-T should have an adequate security apparatus, including policies for fraud and billing.

Carrying ISUP in SIP bodies can invite abuse, fraud and privacy problems, especially when arbitrary endpoints can generate, inspect or modify SIP-T requests. ISUP MIME bodies should be secured, preferably with S/MIME. Signatures let a recipient check that an authorized entity produced the body, and encryption limits inspection to carriers holding the key. SIP-T endpoints MUST support S/MIME signatures (CMS SignedData) and SHOULD support encryption (CMS EnvelopedData). The IANA Considerations section says the document adds nothing for IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret phone-company details inside the call should be sealed and signed, so only the right people can read them and you know who sent them.
